messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Malia, a 35-year-old accountant living in Honolulu with her husband, was walking home from the bus stop one evening when a man came up behind her, grabbed her shoulder, and yanked her purse strap. She turned and saw his face—young, angry, inches from hers—as he shoved her hard against a wall. Her lip split against her teeth, and she tasted blood, sharp and metallic, for hours afterward. He ran off with her bag. The whole thing lasted maybe ten seconds, but it reshaped everything.

In the weeks that followed, Malia found herself unable to stop replaying the moment. She would lie awake at night going over what she could have done differently: walked on the other side of the street, carried her bag across her body instead of loosely over one shoulder, left work earlier. She ruminated endlessly on how it might have been prevented, and each time she landed on a new detail she should have changed, she felt a fresh wave of guilt. It was her fault. The event happened because of the sort of person she was—careless, trusting, too slow to react. The world now felt permanently dangerous, a place where any ordinary street corner could become a trap.

Her memory of the mugging was oddly vivid yet detached. When a sudden smell or sound brought it back, she could taste that metallic blood on her tongue again, as if it were fresh. At the same time, her body would lock into the exact position she had been in when the man grabbed her—shoulders hunched, arms pinned, back against the wall—and she would feel frozen, unable to move or speak. The memory felt so extreme that sometimes she had to remind herself it was real; it was hard to believe it had actually happened to her.

Malia began to develop small but powerful strategies to cope. Whenever a memory surfaced, she would deliberately try to leave her body or blank out, focusing on a spot on the ceiling until the room felt distant and muffled. At work, she found herself constantly listening for footsteps in the hallway behind her desk. If she heard them approaching, her heart would race and she would angle her chair so no one could come up from behind. Two months ago, a colleague tapped her shoulder to ask a question, and she screamed in front of the whole office. After that, she started working with her back to the wall, facing the door.

Her husband told her repeatedly that she was safe, that the mugger was caught and in jail, but Malia could not believe it. Even when she was at home with the doors locked, she could not truly relax. She stayed vigilant, her shoulders tight, scanning for signs of threat. At work, if a spreadsheet took longer to reconcile than expected, her mind would immediately jump to catastrophe—something bad must be happening, someone must be coming for her. Deadlines became a source of dread.

Her avoidance spread. She stopped leaving the office after dark, even though it meant rushing through her closing tasks. She no longer walked to the bus stop; she made her husband pick her up every evening, a routine that strained their evenings and left her feeling dependent and ashamed. She stopped going to grocery stores alone, stopped jogging in the neighborhood park. Her world shrank.

What finally brought Malia to seek help was a panic attack in a client meeting. She had been asked to present a quarterly report, but when a manager asked a follow-up question and paused too long before responding, she felt her chest tighten, tasted blood in her mouth, and had to excuse herself to the restroom, where she sat on the floor dissociating for fifteen minutes. Her husband found her there. That night he told her gently that something had to change. Malia is terrified that she will never feel safe again, but she is also desperate to stop living inside fear—to return to herself, to her work, to a life that does not revolve around what happened in those ten seconds. She wants to believe it is possible, but she is not sure she does yet.
